newsitem.title: USA: Calif. expects above-normal hydroelectric output.
newsitem.headline: Calif. expects above-normal hydroelectric output.

text.p: California is expected to see above-normal precipitation for the water year ending next September, which will mean higher hydroelectric generation, according to preliminary industry forecasts.

"It is still too early to tell for sure, but we are predicting at this time that hydroelectric output should be considerably above normal for 1997," said a Southern California Edison Co's hydrologist.

According to California's Department of Water Resources, automatic sensors showed snowpack in the Sierra Nevada Mountains at 160 percent of average on Monday, although manual measurements will not be made until after January 1.

"We are about 40 percent through the season," said Maury Roos, chief hydrologist at the state agency. "There is a chance that the rain could melt some of the snow, but so far it hasn't had much impact."
Unofficially, Edison is forecasting 1997 runoff at its San Joaquin River projects of 3 million acre feet (maf), or 169 percent of an historical average rate of 1.77 maf.
In 1996, runoff totalled 2.2 maf or 124 percent of average.
Edison has a 50-50 chance of hitting the 3 maf rate next year, while the chances of a normal water year are 9 in 10 and the odds of hitting 4.4 maf are 1 out of 10, their hydrologist said.
If runoff reaches 3 maf, Edison's hydroelectric generation would total around 5,900 gigawatt hours (GWh), compared with a long-term average of 4,800 GWh, according to the utility.
Hydroelectric power often represents the lowest-cost component of utility generation portfolios, and its supply has a major impact on the purchase of other fuels, such as natural gas.
But industry sources caution that January and February remain the wettest months for California, so overall precipitation levels could still shift in either direction.
In addition, precipitation does not directly translate into hydropower generation since runoff is concentrated in the spring and summer months, rather than spread evenly over the year.
Problems such as heavy debris in the runoff and unexpected turbine outages can also impact generation levels.
